speaker: David Vélez
title: How He Built the World’s Largest Digital Bank with 140 Million Customers | David Vélez
question: In retail banking, is massive customer scale by itself enough to create a durable data or AI advantage?
guest: Scale is important, but you also need the right culture and the right systems. In the early days we constantly heard, 'How are you going to compete with the banks? They have a hundred-year history with a hundred million customers—how can you replicate that data?' My answer was always that Blockbuster had a huge amount of data too, watching people walk in and rent DVDs. Did that data help them build a better algorithm? No, because they were not capturing the data, they did not have the right systems to capture it, and they did not have a data culture making decisions based on models. Someone like Netflix could come in with no data and build a better algorithm. That differentiates digitally native organizations from traditional incumbent banks still operating 15 different systems from decades of acquisitions. Today, much of their AI effort is just figuring out how to translate COBOL and get off mainframes after 10 to 15 years of still trying to move to the cloud.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
No. Scale is a necessary ingredient but not a sufficient one. A bank with tens of millions of customers holds a lot of raw data, yet that data is typically fragmented across product silos and legacy core systems, inconsistently labelled, and constrained by privacy and consent rules, so much of it never reaches a model in usable form.

Data also shows diminishing returns: beyond a certain volume, more of the same transaction records adds little predictive power. What matters more is data that is unique, timely and tied to outcomes, such as primary-account transaction flows that reveal income and spending in real time.

Scale's advantage is also eroding from outside. Open banking lets rivals access customer-permissioned data, and cloud and foundation models put strong AI capability within reach of smaller players. Fintechs and neobanks with far fewer customers have often outperformed incumbents in underwriting and personalisation because they have clean, unified data and fast experimentation loops.

The durable advantage comes from combining scale with modern data infrastructure, proprietary feedback loops, AI embedded in real decisions, governance and talent. Scale amplifies those capabilities but cannot replace them.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
No, massive customer scale by itself is not enough to create a durable data or AI advantage in retail banking. Although large incumbents accumulate vast transaction histories, that raw data is frequently trapped across fragmented legacy cores, disconnected product silos, and inconsistent schemas, turning scale into integration debt rather than usable intelligence. Meanwhile, predictive accuracy in core tasks like credit underwriting and servicing often hits diminishing returns beyond moderate sample sizes, and open banking APIs, credit bureaus, shared fraud networks, and commercial foundation models allow smaller challengers to reach strong baseline performance without massive proprietary datasets. Strict privacy, consent, and fair-lending regulations also limit how freely banks can pool customer records across business lines.

Scale becomes a true moat only when paired with unified data architecture, real-time governance, and closed-loop feedback systems that capture proprietary outcomes—such as repayment behavior, fraud resolutions, and offer conversions—and embed them rapidly into production workflows. Without modern infrastructure and agile execution, customer scale remains a dormant asset.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
No. Scale helps, but it isn't enough on its own. A huge customer base gives a bank a lot of raw transaction, deposit and credit data. That data only becomes an edge if the bank can actually use it. In practice the barriers are internal: core systems spread across legacy platforms, poor data quality, siloed product lines, and slow governance that keeps insights from reaching decisions. Many of the largest banks have struggled for exactly these reasons.

Returns on more data also shrink. Beyond a certain volume, extra records add little to fraud or credit model accuracy, and foundation models plus open-banking data access let smaller rivals close much of the gap. Regulation (fair-lending rules, privacy law, model-risk requirements) also limits how freely data can be combined and used.

A lasting advantage comes from scale combined with other things. Those include modern, unified data infrastructure; feedback loops where models shape customer interactions that then produce better data; AI built into everyday workflows; strong talent; and steady investment. JPMorgan's tech budget, now above $17 billion a year, shows the edge comes from the spending and execution, not just the customer count. Scale amplifies capability; it doesn't replace it.
